Each narrative commits to a claim. The last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, the past decade, the past fifty years, since September 2001 and since 1945, that place the day's pattern on longer trajectories. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.

readings.line: Trump called Brazil's election rigged while offering $1 million for evidence of fraud in US elections
readings.claim: Donald Trump made the same accusation about two elections in one news day. He said Brazil's vote, which returned Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro, was rigged, and he pressed claims of fraud in US elections before the midterms with a $1 million reward, a lawsuit and a challenge to 400 ballots. Newspapers in France, Germany, Britain, Korea and Poland carried the Brazil claim, while Nigeria's president and Vladimir Putin congratulated Lula. The foreign accusation matters because it comes from a government preparing to contest results at home, and it presents fraud as the ordinary explanation for a result it dislikes.

fragments.label: Rigged, manipulated, a dirty trick
fragments.text: SudOuest in France and WELT in Germany report Trump calling Brazil's election 'rigged' or 'manipulated' after Flávio Bolsonaro's defeat. The Independent in Britain adds that he said it without evidence, after the incumbent fended off Bolsonaro. Hankyoreh in Seoul puts the claim in the same headline as Netanyahu's own test at the polls, and Onet in Poland reports a 'dirty trick' and says the fight for Brazil is not over.

fragments.label: Congratulations from Abuja and Moscow
fragments.text: Leadership in Nigeria reports Bola Tinubu congratulating Lula and seeking stronger Nigeria-Brazil ties, and Observador in Portugal reports Vladimir Putin's congratulations. Vanguardia in Mexico reads the result as halting the regional shift to the right and denying Trump a powerful ally. An Il Messaggero editorial calls it a signal for Trump. Outside Washington the result was treated as settled.

rungs.label: The same claim about US elections

fragments.label: A reward, a lawsuit, 400 ballots
fragments.text: El Colombiano and Ammon in Jordan report Trump offering $1 million for information leading to convictions for electoral fraud in the US. Yle in Finland reports him filing a lawsuit over what it calls the exposure of multimillion-dollar election rigging. The Hindu reports his administration asking Washington to set aside ballots from 400 voters it says may be non-citizens.

fragments.label: Before a close midterm
fragments.text: Financial News in Seoul describes the midterm polls as a toss-up between a 'blue wave' and a 'ripple'. The Sydney Morning Herald quotes a voter in the Republican heartland saying 'I feel betrayed'. The fraud claims are being made before a vote whose outcome is open.

fragments.label: The foreign case supports the domestic one
fragments.text: The Brazilian claim and the American claims are the same move in two places: a result, or a coming result, is called fraudulent before evidence is shown. Trump's words in Diário do Grande ABC, 'I like Lula, but the extension granted was very strange', place the objection in a procedural detail, which is also how the 400 ballots are framed. Calling a foreign count rigged tells American voters that rigging is a normal explanation for a loss. Netanyahu's open support for Trump, reported by Financial News, shows allies reading each other's elections as one contest.

fragments.label: Brazil moves on to its courts
fragments.text: Inside Brazil the argument has moved from the count to prosecution and policing. Jornal de Brasília quotes Renan Santos expecting a likely arrest of Flávio Bolsonaro, and Diário do Grande ABC reports Guilherme Boulos seeking the arrest of police officers accused of running over a motorcyclist at a pro-Lula rally. El Colombiano profiles André Janones, the digital strategist credited with Lula's comeback, and Estado de Minas reports Santos proposing dialogue after the vote. Brazilian coverage treats the result as finished and its consequences as the story.

fragments.label: One remark, widely copied
fragments.text: Most of the Brazil coverage is one wire story about a single comment, repeated in French, German, Korean and Polish, so ten headlines may rest on one sentence. The 'I like Lula' quote reads as a hedged remark rather than a campaign, and no headline reports any US action against Brazil's result. The reward, the lawsuit and the 400 ballots have a domestic history and would exist without Brazil, so the link may be one of timing in this collection. Translation also flattens the record: 'rigged', 'manipulated' and 'very strange' are different degrees of accusation.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: In 2016 Trump said he would accept the result 'if I win'. After the 2020 vote his campaign and allies lost more than sixty lawsuits, and on 6 January 2021 a crowd stormed the Capitol. Brazil followed the same sequence. Jair Bolsonaro spent years attacking the electronic voting machine, lost to Lula in October 2022 by about 50.9 to 49.1 per cent, and his supporters stormed the buildings of the three branches of government in Brasília on 8 January 2023. Brazil's courts then acted where American ones had not: the electoral court barred Bolsonaro from office for eight years in June 2023, and the Supreme Court convicted him of plotting a coup in September 2025. In July 2025 Washington announced 50 per cent tariffs on Brazilian goods and tied them to his prosecution. By these headlines his son Flávio has now lost as well, and Renan Santos predicts Flávio's arrest. The 'rigged' comment follows a decade in which the US government treated Brazil's electoral and legal process as a matter for its own politics.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: The Carnation Revolution in Lisbon in April 1974 opened what Samuel Huntington in 1991 called the third wave of democratisation, and Brazil was part of it. The generals passed an amnesty in 1979, handed power to a civilian in 1985 and accepted a new constitution in 1988. In 1989 Brazilians elected a president directly for the first time since 1960. In 1996 the electoral court introduced the electronic ballot box, and by 2000 every vote in the country was cast on one. Argentina tried its own juntas in 1985; Brazil chose amnesty, which left the question of military coups unsettled for decades. The September 2025 conviction of a former president for a coup plot was the first time Brazil's courts did what Buenos Aires did in 1985. Trump's complaint in Diário do Grande ABC concerns 'the extension granted', a procedural detail of the system the transition built, and it reaches a country whose electoral court has spent thirty years defending that system against fraud claims of this kind.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: In 2002 the real lost about a third of its value before Lula won at his fourth attempt, and he published a 'Letter to the Brazilian People' promising to honour contracts and debt. His first presidency coincided with left-wing governments across South America, from Néstor Kirchner in Argentina in 2003 to Evo Morales in Bolivia in 2006. The cycle reversed after commodity prices fell in 2014. Dilma Rousseff was impeached in 2016, Lula was jailed in 2018 on a conviction the Supreme Court annulled in 2021, and Bolsonaro won the 2018 election. The right then won Argentina with Javier Milei in 2023 and Chile with José Antonio Kast in 2025. Vanguardia in Mexico reads Lula's 2026 re-election as the end of that regional shift, and Il Messaggero calls it a signal for Trump. El Colombiano credits André Janones, a digital strategist, with the comeback, which places the 2026 contest on social platforms as much as in the currency markets that shaped 2002.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: For most of the post-war period the United States treated Latin American elections as questions of its own security. The Rio Treaty of 1947 bound the hemisphere into a defence pact. The CIA helped remove Guatemala's elected president Jacobo Árbenz in 1954, Washington backed the Brazilian generals who removed João Goulart in March 1964, and after Salvador Allende won in Chile in 1970 Richard Nixon ordered pressure on the Chilean economy. Those interventions were covert or deniable. In the October 2026 headlines the American objection is public, personal and made after the count. Other governments followed the post-war convention of prompt recognition: Bola Tinubu sought stronger Nigeria-Brazil ties and Vladimir Putin sent congratulations, both reported the day after the vote. Brazil has met with Russia, India and China as a bloc since 2009, joined by South Africa in 2010, which gives Lula partners whose recognition does not depend on Washington.

readings.line: Anthropic filed for a record US share listing as Elvis Presley's rights holders sued it over 200 songs
readings.claim: Anthropic's filing with the SEC, which Il Messaggero calls a record and dates to a Nasdaq debut in November, was reported as market news in Singapore, Russia, Korea and New Zealand. In the same news cycle the owners of Elvis Presley's music rights sued the company over more than 200 songs, and a Canadian newspaper attacked Meta's data scraping. Public investors are being asked to buy a company whose title to its training material is in court and whose control, according to CNBC, stays with its founders. The previous edition followed AI through the jobs it removes; Microsoft's severance offer to 60,000 staff continues that thread, but the new development is that the public is now being asked to own a share.

fragments.label: Reported from Singapore to Moscow
fragments.text: CNA in Singapore reports equities ending higher as Anthropic's IPO filing lifted AI stocks. Il Messaggero calls it a record filing with the SEC and gives a Nasdaq debut in November, and Kommersant reports the filing in a one-line headline. Newspim in Seoul reports Wall Street's expectations as mixed and cautious, split between 'expensive' and 'milestone'.

fragments.label: Sales, risks and founders
fragments.text: The NZ Herald reports that the filing shows soaring sales and AI risks. CNBC reports that the listing keeps power with the founders and gives everyday shareholders little voice. The same document asks the public for money, lists the dangers of the product and limits what buyers of shares can decide.

fragments.label: Elvis Presley's songs
fragments.text: BBC News reports that the owners of Elvis Presley's music rights are suing Anthropic for copyright violations. Pulzo in Colombia gives the scale: unauthorised use of more than 200 songs in AI. The suit was reported in the same news cycle as the filing.

fragments.label: Scraping in Canada, hand-made film in New Zealand
fragments.text: A National Post opinion piece says government and industry must push back against Meta's scraping. The NZ Herald presents the stop-motion film 'Wildwood' as a showcase of 'human creativity' in the AI age. Both treat what AI companies take from others, and what people still make by hand, as subjects for public argument.

fragments.label: Contested inputs, closed control
fragments.text: Buyers of Anthropic shares will own a claim on revenue from a product whose training material is contested in court, in a company whose founders keep control. The Elvis suit and the CNBC report describe the two ends of one arrangement: rights holders want a share of what went in, and public shareholders get little say over what comes out. This is what has changed since the previous edition's thread about AI and jobs: the argument has moved to who owns the company and what it was built from.

fragments.label: Chips on one side, staff on the other
fragments.text: The spending goes to hardware. UDN in Taiwan reports SpaceX buying up Nvidia chips, with TSMC and Quanta expected to win orders, and a second UDN report says interposers for advanced packaging have become a sought-after product; CNBC singles out AMD. On the cost side, WELT, Izvestia and Newspim report Microsoft offering about 60,000 employees severance. Izvestia and Newspim tie the offer to AI; WELT's headline does not.

fragments.label: Ordinary lawsuits, ordinary share structures
fragments.text: Copyright suits against AI developers have been filed steadily since 2022, including earlier suits against Anthropic by music publishers and by authors, so one more suit in the week of a filing may be a plaintiff choosing a moment for publicity. Founder control through special share classes has been standard in US technology listings since Google in 2004 and says nothing particular about AI. CNA reports markets rising on the filing, which suggests investors do not see the lawsuits as a threat. The Meta opinion piece concerns a different company in a different country.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei and other former OpenAI staff. ChatGPT's release on 30 November 2022 turned language models into a consumer product, and the lawsuits followed the users. Music publishers including Universal and Concord sued Anthropic in October 2023 over song lyrics, and The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023. In 2025 Judge William Alsup in San Francisco held that training on lawfully bought books was fair use but that keeping pirated copies was not, and Anthropic agreed to pay authors about $1.5 billion, roughly $3,000 a book. In May 2023 the heads of the main laboratories, Anthropic's among them, signed a one-sentence statement that the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority. The NZ Herald report that the filing shows 'soaring sales and AI risks' describes a prospectus that carries both that statement and that legal record. The Elvis suit reported by the BBC and Pulzo concerns recorded music, which the 2025 book settlement did not cover.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: Genentech and Apple went public in October and December 1980, and the two listings set the pattern of investors paying for a technology before its profits. Netscape's offering on 9 August 1995 roughly doubled on its first day for a company with little revenue. The dot-com crash that began in March 2000 took away most of the Nasdaq's value by late 2002 and produced the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, which made executives certify their accounts and lengthened the risk sections of every prospectus. Anthropic's filing, which Il Messaggero calls a record, is read in Singapore by CNA and in Seoul by Newspim the way the 1990s read Netscape: as a price for a whole sector. The difference is revenue. The NZ Herald reports soaring sales, where Netscape had almost none. CNBC's point about founders keeping control belongs to a later practice, the multi-class share structures that the 1980 and 1995 listings did not use.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: After the dot-com crash Google built its business on advertising sold against what users searched for, a model Shoshana Zuboff described in 2019 as surveillance capitalism. Google's 2004 listing gave its founders shares carrying ten votes each. Facebook used a similar structure in 2012, and Snap sold shares with no votes at all in 2017, after which S&P stopped admitting new multi-class companies to its main indices for several years. CNBC's headline about Anthropic's founders keeping power describes this settled Silicon Valley practice. Data collection produced its own reckoning: the Cambridge Analytica revelations and the EU's General Data Protection Regulation both came in 2018. Canada's dispute with Meta sharpened in August 2023, when the company blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in response to the Online News Act. The National Post opinion piece on Meta's scraping continues that dispute, now over material taken to train models rather than to sell advertising.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: For two decades after 1945 the technologies expected to change the world were paid for by states and foundations. The 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth that named artificial intelligence was funded by the Rockefeller Foundation, and after Sputnik in October 1957 the US created ARPA, whose network later became the internet. In the same years the recorded music business that the Elvis lawsuit now defends was built. RCA bought Presley's contract from Sun Records in 1955 for $35,000, and 'Heartbreak Hotel' became his first RCA number one in 1956. A 1971 federal law brought sound recordings under US copyright and the Copyright Act of 1976 extended the terms. A field named in publicly funded research is now listing on the Nasdaq, and one of its disputes is with the owners of recordings from the year it was named. Izvestia's headline attributing Microsoft's 60,000 severance offers to AI repeats an argument about office automation that Norbert Wiener raised in The Human Use of Human Beings in 1950.

readings.line: The Hormuz oil shock is raising US petrol and European gas prices while Iran hosts Gulf security talks
readings.claim: Anadolu reports a CREA analysis that the US paid the heaviest fuel bill in the oil shock driven by the Strait of Hormuz, and The Independent reports US petrol prices above their Biden-era highs. European gas has passed $108 for the first time since 2022, high fuel prices are pushing record sales of new-energy cars in Chile, and Indonesia's rupiah is weakening on oil and the Fed. The price now moves with diplomacy and military threats on the same day: UDN in Taiwan reports oil falling after Iran invited Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey to security talks, while Chinese and Taiwanese outlets report a US official saying the military is ready to strike Iran again. Households in importing countries carry a price set by decisions in Tehran and Washington.

fragments.label: The United States and Europe
fragments.text: Anadolu reports a CREA analysis that the US paid the heaviest fuel bill of any country in the Hormuz-driven oil shock. The Independent reports federal data showing US petrol prices under Trump have passed the highs of the Biden years. Ammon in Jordan reports European gas above $108 for the first time since 2022.

fragments.label: Chile and Indonesia
fragments.text: La Tercera reports that rising petrol and diesel prices keep pushing sales of new-energy cars in Chile to a record. Jawapos reports the rupiah projected to weaken further under pressure from the Fed and oil prices. In both countries the oil price reaches households through a purchase or through the currency.

rungs.label: Talks in Tehran, threats from Washington

fragments.label: The Mecca Alliance in Tehran
fragments.text: Okaz reports representatives of the 'Mecca Agreement' holding talks in Tehran and agreeing to continue dialogue on regional security. Arab News calls it a last-ditch attempt to bring Tehran closer to Makkah. Yicai quotes an Iranian official saying West Asia's security must rely on its own strength, and iefimerida reports Tehran calling for regional unity to avoid a new flare-up. UDN reports Iran inviting Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey to security talks and the easing sending oil prices down.

fragments.label: Ready to strike
fragments.text: NBD in China and ETtoday in Taiwan report a US official saying the military is ready to strike Iran again on a large scale, with ETtoday adding that Trump could order an attack within 96 hours after the election. Al Youm Al Sabe' reports the coalition in Yemen destroying three ballistic missiles and four drones launched by the Houthis, and Walla reports a vessel on fire off Iraq. Arab News reports thousands of trucks stuck as Iran-Pakistan trade only partly resumes.

rungs.label: How countries respond to the price

fragments.label: Using less oil or producing more
fragments.text: The responses differ by country. Chilean buyers are changing cars, while the BBC reports a fight inside Britain's Labour Party over the Rosebank oil field, which is an argument for more domestic supply. Handelsblatt reports EQT buying Range Resources, a consolidation in US shale gas. Each is a way of reducing exposure to a price set by events around Hormuz.

fragments.label: Cheaper power that users do not see
fragments.text: Minuto Uno reports that El Niño has raised Argentina's hydroelectric output and cut energy costs, but not for users. British ministers have announced five 'everyday fixes' for living costs before the Budget, and Corriere della Sera reports Meloni offering talks on the cost of living to all Italian mayors. When generation gets cheaper the saving stays with suppliers, and when fuel gets dearer governments answer with small measures.

fragments.label: Several prices, one named cause
fragments.text: Only the Anadolu report on CREA names Hormuz. The European gas, Chilean fuel and Indonesian currency headlines do not, and Jawapos names the Fed before oil. European gas prices respond to storage levels and winter weather, and Chile's move to new-energy cars has also been driven by falling prices of Chinese cars. CREA is a research group that campaigns against fossil fuels, so its accounting of who paid most has a purpose.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: The Vienna nuclear agreement of July 2015 lifted sanctions on Iranian oil, and Iran's exports recovered to roughly 2.5 million barrels a day by 2018. The US withdrew in May 2018 and reimposed sanctions. In 2019 tankers were attacked near the Strait of Hormuz, and on 14 September drones and missiles struck Abqaiq and briefly halved Saudi output. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 sent European gas to record prices that August, which is why Ammon measures today's European price against 2022. In June 2025 a twelve-day Israel-Iran war ended with American bombers striking Fordow. By these headlines a Hormuz-driven price shock followed in 2026, with CREA reporting that the US paid the heaviest bill. Through the decade each military event around Iran reached consumers within weeks, and UDN's report of oil falling on news of talks in Tehran shows the same transmission working in the other direction.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: In October 1973 Arab producers cut supply and embargoed the US during the Yom Kippur war, and the posted price of oil roughly quadrupled to about $12 a barrel within months. The Iranian revolution of February 1979 caused the second shock, and the price more than doubled again by 1980. Jimmy Carter answered in January 1980 with the doctrine that the US would use force to keep the Gulf open. During the Iran-Iraq war the tanker war of 1984 to 1988 led the US to reflag Kuwaiti tankers in 1987 and escort them through Hormuz. The 1970s also produced the tools governments still use: the International Energy Agency in 1974, strategic stocks and fuel-economy rules for cars. Chile's record new-energy car sales, reported by La Tercera, repeat the 1970s response of buying less oil, and Daniel Yergin's The Prize records how each shock was followed by a round of substitution.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: The invasion of Iraq in March 2003 removed Iran's main regional rival and opened a period of high prices; Brent crude reached $147 a barrel in July 2008. High prices paid for the American shale boom, which used horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to lift US crude output from about 5 million barrels a day in 2008 to more than 12 million in 2019, when the US began exporting more petroleum than it imported. Handelsblatt's report of EQT buying Range Resources is consolidation in the Appalachian shale gas fields developed in those years. Shale did not protect American drivers, because oil is priced in a world market. CREA's finding that the US paid the heaviest fuel bill in 2026 reflects how much fuel the US burns rather than how much it imports. The Independent's comparison with 'Biden-era highs' refers to June 2022, when the US average for petrol passed $5 a gallon.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: On 14 February 1945 Franklin Roosevelt met King Abdulaziz Ibn Saud aboard the USS Quincy in the Great Bitter Lake, and the unwritten exchange of American protection for Saudi oil shaped the Gulf for eighty years. In February 1955 Iraq and Turkey signed the Baghdad Pact, which Britain, Pakistan and Iran joined within the year as an alliance against the Soviet Union. In 1956 the Suez crisis ended British power in the region and confirmed American power. The capitals in the 2026 headlines are close to the 1955 list: UDN reports Iran inviting Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey to security talks, and Okaz reports the 'Mecca Alliance' meeting in Tehran to keep a diplomatic path open. The place of Washington has changed. The Baghdad Pact was built around American interests. The Tehran talks take place while NBD and ETtoday report a US official saying the military is ready to strike, and Yicai quotes an Iranian official saying the region's security must rely on its own strength.

readings.line: Students are on strike or occupying buildings in France, Mexico, India and Italy, with Serbia next
readings.claim: Students are striking or occupying in France, Mexico, India and Italy this week, and their demands concern how education is run: conditions and the Parcoursup admissions platform in France, a date for polls at Jamia Millia Islamia in Delhi, a philosophy faculty taken over at the Autonomous University of Querétaro, a school occupation in Rome. The French government has met some demands, which outlets in Ukraine, Germany and Turkey report, but the second French story is about the police and the far right. In Serbia, where the opposition has won, ANSA reports the new government now facing the students. The movements are winning partial concessions on administration while the political advantage of the disorder goes, in these reports, to others.

fragments.label: Partial concessions, reported abroad
fragments.text: LB.ua in Ukraine and WELT in Germany report the French government agreeing to meet some demands of the student and school protests. Anadolu reports calls in France for students to keep protesting for better education conditions. The concession and the call to continue were reported together.

fragments.label: Parcoursup and the unrest
fragments.text: A SudOuest editorial calls Parcoursup, the national university admissions platform, 'the perfect culprit'. El País English sends a reporter to what it calls the ground zero of the unrest in France. The French dispute is about how places in higher education are allocated.

fragments.label: Querétaro, Delhi and Rome
fragments.text: Excélsior reports a student strike at the Autonomous University of Querétaro, with the philosophy faculty taken over and classes suspended. The Tribune reports Jamia students refusing to end their protest on its sixteenth day until they get a definite date for polls. Corriere della Sera reports students at a school in Tor Bella Monaca accusing the headteacher of shoves and slaps during their occupation, and a circular calling Italy an 'intolerant and xenophobic state' becoming a case at a high school in Salò.

fragments.label: Serbia after the vote
fragments.text: ANSA reports that Serbia has turned the page and that the new government now faces a challenge from the students. Izvestia considers what Russia can expect from the opposition's victory, and Lenta reports a post-Soviet leader addressing Serbia's new authorities. The Serbian student movement has reached the stage that follows a change of government.

fragments.label: Places, polls and buildings
fragments.text: These are disputes about administration: who gets a university place in France, when polls are held at Jamia, who controls a faculty in Querétaro or a school in Rome. The state's control of places appears elsewhere in the collection. Izvestia reports Russia's science ministry fixing the number and structure of state-funded places for 2027-28, and DW reports Syria banning women from university courses. In Bangladesh a human chain on the Kushtia Zilla School ground demanded a halt to political programmes held there.

fragments.label: The far right and the police
fragments.text: Milenio in Mexico argues that the protests in Paris benefit the far right. Franceinfo reports witnesses saying violent far-right activists passed through the CRS riot police without trouble during Saturday's protests, and asks whether they were spared. The students win concessions on admissions, and in these reports the political benefit of the disorder goes to parties opposed to them.

fragments.label: Serbia read from Moscow
fragments.text: In Serbia the students' side has won, and the question is what the new government owes them. Russian outlets read the change through Russia's interests: Izvestia asks what Moscow can expect, and Lenta reports a post-Soviet leader speaking to the new authorities. A student movement that brings down a government becomes a foreign-policy story for its neighbours.

fragments.label: Autumn protests are routine
fragments.text: French school and university protests follow the start of the academic year almost every autumn, and a partial concession is their usual ending. The Jamia dispute concerns campus elections, a recurring issue, and the Querétaro and Rome occupations are local disputes with no stated connection to each other or to France. Coverage of France in Ukrainian, German, Turkish, Mexican and Spanish outlets inflates its weight in this collection. Syria's ban runs the other way, a state closing courses rather than students taking buildings, and belongs to a different story.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: The decade's student movements began with specific grievances. In South Africa in 2015 students under the name Fees Must Fall forced a freeze in university fees. In France the Orientation and Student Success law of March 2018 replaced the APB admissions system with Parcoursup, which lets universities rank applicants; SudOuest's editorial calls it 'the perfect culprit' eight years later. In July 2024 students in Dhaka protesting job quotas forced Sheikh Hasina from power by early August. On 1 November 2024 the station canopy at Novi Sad collapsed and killed sixteen people, and Serbian students began blockades of faculties that, by these headlines, ended in an opposition victory in October 2026. In September 2025 young protesters in Kathmandu brought down a government after it banned social media platforms. ANSA's report that Serbia's new government now faces the students marks the point Bangladesh's movement reached in 2025: a movement without a party finding that the government formed after its victory is also its target.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: On 16 June 1976 schoolchildren in Soweto marched against teaching in Afrikaans, and the police killings that followed began the long end of apartheid. In France the 1986 Devaquet bill, which would have let universities select students and raise fees, was withdrawn in December after weeks of protest and the death of the student Malik Oussekine following a police beating in Paris. Selection at entry has been the most reliable trigger of French student protest since, and Parcoursup is its current form. In June 1987 students and office workers in Seoul won direct presidential elections. Enrolment grew everywhere: India's university population passed 40 million in the 2020s. Jamia Millia Islamia became a central university by an act of parliament in 1988, and police entered its campus in December 2019 during protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act. That history is why a sixteen-day protest there over polls, reported by The Tribune, is followed closely.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: In November 2003 Georgia's Rose Revolution copied the methods of Serbia's Otpor student movement, and Moscow concluded that street movements are organised from abroad. That reading is still visible in the Russian coverage of Serbia, where Izvestia considers what Russia can expect from the opposition's victory. In France in 2006 students and school pupils forced the government to withdraw the first-job contract, the CPE, after it had been passed. In Cairo in 2011 the young held Tahrir Square for eighteen days and won, then lost the outcome to the army in 2013. Mexican student protest carries a particular memory: in September 2014, 43 students from the Ayotzinapa teacher-training college disappeared in Iguala. The strike at Querétaro reported by Excélsior takes place in a country whose interior ministry, in a Milenio headline the same day, denies UN action against Mexico over disappearances. Albert Hirschman's distinction between exit and voice describes the choice each of these movements faced after winning or losing.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: European and Latin American universities grew several times over after 1945 as states paid for mass secondary and higher education, and the first large generation to reach them produced 1968. In Paris in May 1968 students and then about ten million strikers stopped the country; the government answered with the Faure law of November 1968, which reorganised the universities and gave students elected seats on their councils. In Mexico City on 2 October 1968 the army fired on students at Tlatelolco ten days before the Olympics. In Belgrade that June students occupied the university, and Tito made concessions in a televised speech. On 5 October 2000 Otpor's students helped bring down Slobodan Milošević. The French concession reported by LB.ua and WELT follows the Faure pattern of reform after protest, and franceinfo's question about whether police spared far-right activists repeats the 1968 argument about whom the police protect. Serbian students in 2026 act in a country with both the 1968 and the 2000 precedent.

readings.line: Egypt, Indonesia and Tamil Nadu are expanding housing while Portugal investigates police at housing protests
readings.claim: Governments in Egypt, Indonesia and India's Tamil Nadu are adding housing through state schemes and looser building rules, and in Germany companies short of skilled workers are building homes for them. At the same time DWS has limited withdrawals from its largest open-ended property fund as rates rise, and in Portugal the Ombudsman and the police inspectorate are examining how the PSP handled housing protests in Lisbon and Porto. The headlines show housing being supplied less by private investment and more by states and employers, with protest where neither reaches enough people.

fragments.label: Egypt and Indonesia
fragments.text: Al Watan reports the booking link for the ninth round of 'Housing for All Egyptians' closing within hours, and tells readers it is the last chance to apply. Liputan6 reports Housing Minister Maruarar meeting President Prabowo to discuss the 2026 targets of the Bedah Rumah home renovation programme. In both countries the state allocates housing directly.

fragments.label: Tamil Nadu and Kumamoto
fragments.text: ETRealty reports Tamil Nadu raising its building height limit to 19.5 metres and easing rules in the Chennai aquifer zone. 47NEWS reports Kumamoto Prefecture publishing a draft recovery plan that rushes to rebuild housing and livelihoods. Indian deregulation and Japanese reconstruction are both state decisions about where homes go.

fragments.label: Company flats and a restricted fund
fragments.text: WELT reports German companies short of skilled workers turning to company housing. Handelsblatt reports DWS restricting redemptions from its largest open-ended property fund, and in a separate report says rising interest rates are catching up with Europe's governments through the bond market. Employers are building homes while a private property fund holds on to investors' money.

fragments.label: Police at Portugal's housing protests
fragments.text: SAPO reports the Ombudsman urgently asking the PSP for information on its deployment in Lisbon and Porto, and the police inspectorate IGAI opening an investigation into PSP conduct at the protests. 24 Notícias quotes a constitutional law expert arguing that police action at the housing protests did not violate the right to demonstrate. Portuguese outlets treat the policing of housing protests as a constitutional question.

fragments.label: States and employers take over
fragments.text: The common question is who supplies homes. Egypt and Indonesia allocate them, German employers build them for the workers they need, and a large German property fund limits withdrawals as rates rise. Where private investment slows, states and employers take on the job, and Portugal shows the protest that follows when neither covers enough people. Karl Polanyi's account of societies pulling land and labour back from the market when it fails them fits these cases.

fragments.label: Coastlines, aquifers and farms
fragments.text: 163.com asks who will get the last stretch of Qingdao's coastline after thirty years of the city expanding east, and reports the renewal of commercial units around Shanghai's Jin Mao Tower. Martinique La 1ère reports farmers at Morne-Rouge mobilising against the sale of the land they farm. Tamil Nadu has opened Chennai's aquifer zone to more building. In each case land for homes and offices comes from another use: farmland, groundwater recharge or coastline.

fragments.label: The view from Banpo
fragments.text: Herald Economy reports that a second-generation estate agent who has worked in Seoul's Banpo district for 47 years has published a short story collection titled 'The Bare Face of the Rich'. In one of the most expensive housing districts in Korea, the person who brokers the deals writes about the owners. It is the private-market end of the same subject the Egyptian and Indonesian schemes address from the state's side.

fragments.label: Different problems under one word
fragments.text: German open-ended property funds such as DWS's hold mainly offices and shops, so the redemption limit says more about commercial property and interest rates than about homes. Egypt's scheme is in its ninth round, an established programme rather than a new turn, and Tamil Nadu's higher height limit is deregulation, the opposite of state provision. The Portuguese inquiries concern police conduct and may say more about policing than about housing. The pattern depends on reading 'housing' in very different headlines as one subject.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: From 2014 the European Central Bank held its deposit rate below zero, and savers looking for income moved money into property, including German open-ended property funds. The ECB began raising rates in July 2022 and reached 4 per cent in September 2023, and the Handelsblatt reports on rising bond yields and on DWS restricting redemptions describe the end of that period for property. In Portugal the golden visa, introduced in 2012, and short-term letting through platforms pushed up Lisbon rents through the decade; the 2023 Mais Habitação package ended golden visas for property purchases and restricted new short-term lets. Egypt's state housing drive expanded from 2014, and Al Watan's report of a ninth booking round shows a programme now run as a routine. Germany's Skilled Immigration Act took effect in 2020, and WELT's report of companies building housing for recruits shows the limit of that law: a work visa does not come with a flat near the factory.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: After the Carnation Revolution of April 1974 residents occupied empty houses in Lisbon and Porto, and the SAAL programme let neighbourhood associations build their own homes with architects such as Álvaro Siza. The 1976 constitution gave every Portuguese citizen a right to housing, which today's protesters invoke and which the constitutional expert in 24 Notícias weighs against the police's actions. Elsewhere the half-century moved housing from states to markets. Britain's Housing Act of 1980 let council tenants buy their homes, and China ended the allocation of housing through work units in 1998 and built a private property market. Pudong, where 163.com reports the renewal around the Jin Mao Tower, was opened for development in 1990. Egypt kept Nasser-era rent controls while Sadat's open-door policy from 1974 encouraged private building. The company housing in WELT revives, on a small scale, the employer model that China and Britain dismantled.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: Cheap credit after 2001 built housing booms in the US, Spain and Ireland, and the failure of Lehman Brothers on 15 September 2008 turned the boom into a crash. Spanish banks repossessed hundreds of thousands of homes, and on 15 May 2011 the indignados camped in Madrid's Puerta del Sol; Podemos, which grew out of that movement, later entered government without bringing rents down. German open-ended property funds faced heavy withdrawals in 2008 and several were wound up in the following years, and the Capital Investment Code of 2013 required new investors to hold units for 24 months and give twelve months' notice before redeeming. DWS restricting redemptions, by the Handelsblatt headline, is that code in use. Adam Tooze's Crashed traces how the 2008 crisis moved from mortgages into politics. Portugal's housing protests, and the Ombudsman's questions about police in Lisbon and Porto, follow from the 2011 bailout and the rent liberalisation of 2012.

horizons.label: How we got here
horizons.text: In 1945 about a fifth of Germany's housing stock had been destroyed or badly damaged, and West Germany built around half a million homes a year through the 1950s, much of it social housing and much of it by employers and trade-union companies. Neue Heimat, the union-owned builder, became one of Europe's largest housing companies before collapsing in scandal in 1982. German company housing goes back to Krupp's estates in Essen in the nineteenth century, and Volkswagen's town of Wolfsburg was built around its factory. Japan created the Japan Housing Corporation in 1955 and rebuilt with public estates, and the draft Kumamoto recovery plan reported by 47NEWS follows that tradition of prefecture-led rebuilding. Tony Judt's Postwar describes the European state that took responsibility for housing after 1945. The WELT report of companies turning to company housing to attract skilled workers is a small return to the employer's role of the 1950s, made because neither the state nor the market has built enough homes near the jobs.
